title: Why Are 38 Percent of Stanford Students Saying They\x26#39;re Disabled?
titleZh: 为什么38%的斯坦福学生自称残障
summary:
美国精英大学的学生理应是全美最具才智和发展潜力的年轻人，但如今，他们之中却有相当高比例的人在申请原本为学习障碍学生所设的学业便利措施。本周，《大西洋月刊》刊登了教育记者罗斯·霍洛维奇的报道，披露了几组令人惊讶的数据。在布朗大学和哈佛大学，20%的本科生自报存在某种障碍。在阿默斯特学院，这一比例达到了34%。而斯坦福大学的比例更是达到惊人的38%。这些学生申报的障碍大多与心理健康及学习困难相关，包括焦虑、抑郁以及注意力缺陷多动障碍（ADHD）等。

来源：Reason；作者：Emma Camp；原文发布时间：2025-12-05 20:00:00

paragraphs.contentEn: The students at America's elite universities are supposed to be the smartest, most promising young people in the country. And yet, shocking percentages of them are claiming academic accommodations designed for students with learning disabilities. In an article published this week in The Atlantic, education reporter Rose Horowitch lays out some shocking numbers. At Brown and Harvard, 20 percent of undergraduate students are disabled. At Amherst College, that's 34 percent. At Stanford University, it's a galling 38 percent. Most of these students are claiming mental health conditions and learning disabilities, like anxiety, depression, and ADHD.
paragraphs.contentZh: 美国精英大学的学生理应是全美最具才智和发展潜力的年轻人，但如今，他们之中却有相当高比例的人在申请原本为学习障碍学生所设的学业便利措施。本周，《大西洋月刊》刊登了教育记者罗斯·霍洛维奇的报道，披露了几组令人惊讶的数据。在布朗大学和哈佛大学，20%的本科生自报存在某种障碍。在阿默斯特学院，这一比例达到了34%。而斯坦福大学的比例更是达到惊人的38%。这些学生申报的障碍大多与心理健康及学习困难相关，包括焦虑、抑郁以及注意力缺陷多动障碍（ADHD）等。

paragraphs.contentEn: Obviously, something is off here. The idea that some of the most elite, selective universities in America—schools that require 99th percentile SATs and sterling essays—would be educating large numbers of genuinely learning disabled students is clearly bogus. A student with real cognitive struggles is much more likely to end up in community college, or not in higher education at all, right?
paragraphs.contentZh: 情况很显然有些反常。如果说美国那些最顶尖、录取标准最严苛的大学——要求SAT成绩进入前1%、申请文书必须无可挑剔的学校——正在招收大量确实存在学习障碍的学生，这一说法显然站不住脚。毕竟，在认知方面真正存在困难的学生，更可能就读社区大学，甚至无法进入高等教育，不是吗？

paragraphs.contentEn: The professors Horowitz interviewed largely back up this theory. "You hear 'students with disabilities' and it's not kids in wheelchairs," one professor told Horowitch. "It's just not. It's rich kids getting extra time on tests." Talented students get to college, start struggling, and run for a diagnosis to avoid bad grades. Ironically, the very schools that cognitively challenged students are most likely to attend—community colleges—have far lower rates of disabled students, with only three to four percent of such students getting accommodations. To be fair, some of the students receiving these accommodations do need them. But the current language of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) allows students to get expansive accommodations with little more than a doctor's note.
paragraphs.contentZh: 霍洛维奇采访的教授们在很大程度上印证了这一判断。 一名教授告诉她：“如今提到‘残障学生’，不要只想到坐轮椅来上课的孩子。完全不是。更多时候，不过是一些家境优渥的学生，借此在考试中争取额外时间。”许多原本成绩优异的学生进入大学后，一旦遇到挫折，便会急于寻求诊断，以避免拿到难看的成绩。讽刺的是，在那些真正有认知困难的学生更可能就读的学校（社区大学）里，被认定为残障学生的比例反而低得多，享受学术便利措施的只有大约3%到4%的学生。当然，确实有一部分学生真正需要这些支持。但依照现行《美国残疾人法案》（ADA）的规定，学生只需一份医生开具的证明，就能相对轻易地获得范围相当宽泛的学术便利。

paragraphs.contentEn: While some students are no doubt seeking these accommodations as semi-conscious cheaters, I think most genuinely identify with the mental health condition they're using to get extra time on tests. Over the past few years, there's been a rising push to see mental health and neurodevelopmental conditions as not just a medical fact, but an identity marker. Will Lindstrom, the director of the Regents' Center for Learning Disorders at the University of Georgia, told Horowitch that he sees a growing number of students with this perspective. "It's almost like it's part of their identity," Lindstrom told her. "By the time we see them, they're convinced they have a neurodevelopmental disorder."
paragraphs.contentZh: 其中固然有少数学生在申请学术便利时抱有投机心理，但我认为，大多数学生确实认同自己用来争取考试延时的那种心理健康诊断。过去几年，人们越来越倾向于将心理健康和神经发育类问题，不仅视为医学事实，更看作一种身份标识。佐治亚大学董事会下属的学习障碍中心主任威尔·林德斯特伦告诉霍洛维奇，他看到持有这种看法的学生正在不断增多。林德斯特伦告诉她：“这几乎成了他们自我认同的一部分。等他们来到我们这里时，已经深信自己患有某种神经发育障碍。”

paragraphs.contentEn: What's driving this trend? Well, the way conditions like ADHD, autism, and anxiety get talked about online—the place where most young people first learn about these conditions—is probably a contributing factor. Online creators tend to paint a very broad picture of the conditions they describe. A quick scroll of TikTok reveals creators labeling everything from always wearing headphones, to being bad at managing your time, to doodling in class as a sign that someone may have a diagnosable condition. According to these videos, who isn't disabled?
paragraphs.contentZh: 是什么在推动这一趋势？像ADHD、自闭症和焦虑症这类病症在网络上的讨论方式——而这正是大多数年轻人最初了解这些问题的渠道——很可能是原因之一。网络内容创作者往往将这些病症的表现描绘得极其宽泛。随便刷一刷TikTok，你就会看到，有人把总是戴着耳机、时间管理能力差甚至上课时涂涂画画这类行为，都标记为可能与某种可诊断的病症相关。按照这些视频的逻辑，这世上还有谁不算障碍者？

paragraphs.contentEn: The result is a deeply distorted view of "normal." If ever struggling to focus or experiencing boredom is a sign you have ADHD, the implication is that a "normal," nondisabled person has essentially no problems. A "neurotypical" person, the thinking goes, can churn out a 15-page paper with no hint of procrastination, maintain perfect focus during a boring lecture, and never experience social anxiety or awkwardness. This view is buffeted by the current way many of these conditions are diagnosed. As Horowitch points out, when the latest issue of the DSM, the manual psychiatrists use to diagnose patients, was released in 2013, it significantly lowered the bar for an ADHD diagnosis. When the definition of these conditions is set so liberally, it's easy to imagine a highly intelligent Stanford student becoming convinced that any sign of academic struggle proves they're learning disabled, and any problems making friends are a sign they have autism.
paragraphs.contentZh: 最终的结果是，人们对“正常”的认知被严重扭曲。如果一时难以集中注意力或偶尔感到无聊就被视为ADHD的迹象，那么这种推论意味着，一个“正常”的、没有障碍的人本质上不该遇到任何问题。按照这种逻辑，“神经典型者”理应能够毫不拖延地写完一篇15页的论文，在枯燥的课堂上始终保持专注，从不会经历社交焦虑或感到尴尬。而当前许多此类病症的诊断方式，也在强化这种认知。正如霍洛维奇所指出，当精神科医生用来诊断患者的《精神障碍诊断与统计手册》（DSM）新版于2013年发布时，其中对ADHD的诊断门槛被大幅降低。在如此宽泛的定义之下，我们不难想象一位极其聪明的斯坦福学生，可能会把任何学业上的困难都视为自己存在学习障碍，把任何交友上的困难都解读为自闭症的征兆。

paragraphs.contentEn: Risk-aversion, too, seems like a compelling factor driving bright students to claim learning disabilities. Our nation's most promising students are also its least assured. So afraid of failure—of bad grades, of a poorly-received essay—they take any sign of struggle as a diagnosable condition. A few decades ago, a student who entered college and found the material harder to master and their time less easily managed than in high school would have been seen as relatively normal. Now, every time she picks up her phone, a barrage of influencers is clamoring to tell her this is a sign she has ADHD. Discomfort and difficulty are no longer perceived as typical parts of growing up.
paragraphs.contentZh: 规避风险的心态，似乎也是促使这些聪明学生主动寻求学习障碍诊断的一个重要因素。这个国家最有潜力的年轻人，往往也最缺乏安全感。他们极度害怕失败——害怕成绩不佳，害怕论文得不到认可——于是将学习上的任何困难，都视为一种可被诊断的病症。放在几十年前，一名刚进入大学的学生如果发现课程比高中更难掌握、时间也更难管理，人们会认为这是相当正常的情况。而现在，每当她拿起手机，铺天盖地的网红博主都在告诉她，这就是ADHD的迹象。不适与困难，已不再被视为成长过程中的自然组成部分。

paragraphs.contentEn: In this context, it's easy to read the rise of academic accommodations among the nation's most intelligent students as yet another manifestation of the risk-aversion endemic in the striving children of the upper middle class. For most of the elite-college students who receive them, academic accommodations are a protection against failure and self-doubt. Unnecessary accommodations are a two-front form of cheating—they give you an unjust leg-up on your fellow students, but they also allow you to cheat yourself out of genuine intellectual growth. If you mask learning deficiencies with extra time on texts, soothe social anxiety by forgoing presentations, and neglect time management skills with deadline extensions, you might forge a path to better grades. But you'll also find yourself less capable of tackling the challenges of adult life.
paragraphs.contentZh: 在这样的背景下，全美最聪明的学生中涌现出的学术便利申请热潮，很容易被解读为在中上阶层那些奋力向上的子女中普遍存在的风险规避心态的另一种表现。对大多数在精英大学获得这些便利的学生来说，这层保护让他们避免失败和自我怀疑。然而，这些多余的便利本质上是一种双重作弊——既在竞争中获取了不公平的优势，也让他们在自欺欺人中错失了真正的心智成长。如果你依赖考试加时来掩盖学习上的不足，通过回避演讲来缓解社交焦虑，借助作业延期来逃避时间管理的挑战，你或许能换来一份更漂亮的成绩单。 但最终你会发现，在面对成人世界的种种挑战时，自己已难以应对。
